newsitem.title: USA: SF Fed economist sees dlr holding onto lead status.
newsitem.headline: SF Fed economist sees dlr holding onto lead status.

text.p: The U.S. dollar should retain its status as the premier world currency despite increased use of the yen in international transactions, an economist with the Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco said.
"For now, it looks as though the dollar has a role to play and it will play it for some time," San Francisco Fed senior economist Ramon Moreno told Reuters in an interview.

"This doesn't mean that incrementally the yen's share in international use won't rise, but there is nothing on the horizon to change the dollar's role substantially," said Moreno, who discussed an article appearing in the Oct 18 edition of the San Francisco Fed's "Economic Letter."
He said there is a certain amount of inertia to the dollar's status as a lead currency that would make its replacement unlikely, barring any dramatic developments.

"Once people start using a currency it's costly to switch to another currency," Moreno said. "My basic impression is that you would need a really big event to change the situation that we observe now."

Likening the dollar's situation to that of the British pound early this century, Moreno said sterling's status changed only after a major shift in the relative importance of the U.K. economy and two world wars. "It was a number of big events, and events like that are impossible to predict."
Concerning the expanded role for the yen, Moreno referred in his article to figures showing that its share in invoicing international trade transactions has grown.

"Between 1970 and 1994, the share of the yen in invoicing Japan's own exports rose sharply, from about one percent to nearly 40 percent, while the dollar's share fell from 90 percent to around 50 percent," Moreno wrote.
Still, he said the yen's share in Japan's exports remains considerably lower than the share of the mark in German exports, which he said exceeded 80 percent in the late 1980s.

The yen's share in some kinds of international lending has also risen, Moreno said. Another factor he said could influence the yen's role was the stability of its purchasing power, which has enhanced the currency's attractiveness.
On the other hand, Moreno said that to a certain extent, the volatility of the dollar/yen exchange rate may have limited the yen's use in world financial markets.
He also said the fact that Japan's financial markets are less liquid and deep than U.S. markets posed a limitation to the yen's use as an international currency.
Overall, Moreno said that despite the increased use of the yen, "there is no sign of a broad shift away from the dollar in global markets."
Asked about the potential for the planned new European euro currency to challenge the dollar's role internationally, Moreno played down that possibility as well.
"There are a lot of fundamental issues that need to be resolved," Moreno said, stressing that economic conditions are an important determining factor.
"You don't see dynamism in Europe that you do in Asia and some other areas of the world," he said.
